query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Oxidation resistance often controls the life of high temperature alloys in structural engineering applications. Dense, continuous and adherent Al2O3 or SiO2 oxides protect alloys from oxidation at high temperatures (T > 1000 °C). These oxides are the most protective, because of their high thermodynamic stability and the low diffusivities for anions and cations. Unfortunately, Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina formers, because in these alloys the concentration of Al must be kept low owing to the adverse effect of this element on mechanical properties (ductile to brittle transition temperature-DBTT of the Nbss, toughness, high temperature strength and creep of the alloy). Furthermore, the concentration of Si in these alloys, which can be as high as 20 at.%, cannot assure the formation of silica scale. In other words, the Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina or silica formers. Instead, their scales consist of Ti niobates, AlNbO4, CrNbO4 and oxides of Nb and Ti [,].

The literature on the oxidation of Ti–Al alloys shows that protective Al2O3 scale does not necessarily form when alumina is thermodynamically stable in the alloy and that higher Al concentrations are required for kinetic reasons []. In other words, there are “two” Al concentrations, one required to thermodynamically stabilise Al2O3, we shall call this CtherAl, and the other, which we shall call CkinAl (CkinAl ≥ CtherAl), required to form a continuous protective oxide. Thermodynamics dominate alumina formation when CkinAl = CtherAl and kinetics when CkinAl > CtherAl. The same is the case for Ti–Si alloys where the minimum Si concentration to form SiO2 is about 40 to 45 at.% []. Alloying additions may change CtherAl, the oxygen solubility and the diffusivities of oxygen and Al in the alloy and thus may affect the concentration of Al at the oxide/alloy interface (see discussion). Kinetic factors would reduce CkinAl − CtherAl (for example, see in previous section comment about the addition of Nb in Ti–48Al). Some Nb-based alloys (not Nb-silicide based alloys) with high concentrations of Ti, Al, and Cr have good oxidation resistance in the 800–1200 °C range, approaching that of the oxidation-resistant superalloys []. In Nb-silicide based alloys the alloying additions of (i) Al, B, Cr, Fe, Ge, Hf, Si, Sn or Ti individually and in synergy have a strong effect on the compositions and properties of phases, for example see reference [,,,,], and can improve the oxidation resistance of the alloys significantly [,,,,,,,], (ii) B, Ge or Sn are very effective for suppressing pest oxidation in Nb-silicide based alloys [,] and (iii) refractory metals significantly improve high temperature strength and creep [], are not detrimental to oxidation at low concentrations [,], and have a strong effect on the composition of the Nbss [,]. A successful coating for Nb-silicide based alloy must demonstrate (i) low growth rate of the protective oxide layer, (ii) resistance to cracking, (iii) low evaporation rates of the protective oxide and other coating constituents, (iv) minimum coating-substrate interdiffusion and (v) self-healing ability.
